extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, merchants, economists, and students of political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and criteria for trade policy (drawbacks, bounties, balance of trade/produce) as articulated in a classical political-economy text. Focuses on when export encouragements are justified and their likely economic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of rich neighbours for foreign trade
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation that would enrich itself by foreign trade, is certainly most likely to do so, when its neighbours are all rich, industrious and commercial nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: A rich neighbour affords a better market for immediate produce or for what is purchased with that produce; competition from manufacturers of a rich nation can be dangerous to rival manufacturers but benefits the great body of people by creating a larger market and circulating more capital. Policy implication: favouring impoverishment of neighbours is self-defeating; fostering mutually prosperous neighbours increases beneficial trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of produce and consumption determines national prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: This is the balance of the annual produce and consumption: if the exchangeable value of the annual produce exceeds that of the annual consumption, the capital of the society must annually increase; if it falls short, the capital must annually decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes this balance from the balance of trade: it may take place in a nation with no foreign trade and can operate for the whole globe. Policy should aim to increase exchangeable annual produce relative to consumption to grow capital, rather than focusing solely on mercantile balance of trade figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of produce can improve despite an adverse balance of trade
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance of produce and consumption may be constantly in favour of a nation, though what is called the balance of trade be generally against it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a nation may import more than it exports for decades while its real wealth (exchangeable value of annual produce) grows. Do not equate an unfavourable balance of trade with national impoverishment; evaluate real annual produce and capital accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawbacks as reasonable encouragements to exportation
rubrics_metrics.description: To allow the merchant to draw back upon exportation, either the whole, or a part of whatever excise or inland duty is imposed upon domestic industry, can never occasion the exportation of a greater quantity of goods than what would have been exported had no duty been imposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawbacks do not change the natural distribution of labour but prevent duties from driving capital away; they 'preserve' the natural division of labour. Use drawbacks to neutralize distortions caused by internal duties rather than to create new artificial advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope for drawbacks — foreign independent markets
rubrics_metrics.description: These reasons will justify drawbacks only upon exporting goods to those countries which are altogether foreign and independent, not to those in which our merchants and manufacturers enjoy a monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a monopoly already guarantees export markets (e.g., colonies with preferential treatment), drawbacks may be pure revenue losses without increasing exports. Apply drawbacks selectively where they truly expand exports to independent foreign markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-fraud constraint on drawbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawbacks are useful only in those cases in which the goods, for the exportation of which they are given, are really exported to some foreign country, and not clandestinely re-imported into our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical warning: historical abuses (e.g., tobacco drawbacks) show frequent frauds. Administrative safeguards and enforcement are required; otherwise drawbacks harm revenue and honest traders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carrying trade: no special encouragement but should not be precluded
rubrics_metrics.description: The carrying trade, though it deserves no peculiar encouragement, ought not to be precluded, but to be left free, like all other trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: carrying trade provides employment for otherwise idle capital and foreign freight often brings in money from foreigners. Drawbacks that prevent duties from excluding carrying trade are justifiable, but special bounties or privileges are unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties justified only for uneconomic trades
rubrics_metrics.description: Bounties...ought to be given to those branches of trade only which cannot be carried on without them. Every branch...in which the merchant can sell his goods for a price which replaces to him, with the ordinary profits of stock, the whole capital...can be carried on without a bounty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: only subsidize trades where, without subsidy, the price does not replace capital plus ordinary profit (i.e., merchant forced to sell below full cost). Do not subsidize trades that are already economically viable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties distort comparative advantage and force trade into worse channels
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of bounties, like that of all the other expedients of the mercantile system, can only be to force the trade of a country into a channel much less advantageous than that in which it would naturally run of its own accord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bounties can create persistent losing trades and misallocate capital. Long-term national benefit requires allowing capital to follow natural comparative advantage rather than government-paid distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties raise domestic prices and impose twofold taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The corn bounty...imposes two different taxes upon the people; first, the tax which they are obliged to contribute, in order to pay the bounty; and, secondly, the tax which arises from the advanced price of the commodity in the home market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantified example: a modest bounty can raise home prices so that the population pays much more in aggregate than the subsidy cost. Effects include reduced subsistence for labouring poor or higher wages (which burden employers) and long-term restraint on population and industry. Policy must consider distributional and second-order price effects, not only direct fiscal cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounties affect nominal but not real prices (degrading currency value)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the real, but the nominal price of corn, which can in any considerable degree be affected by the bounty...The real effect of the bounty is not so much to raise the real value of corn, as to degrade the real value of silver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: bounties tend to change money-prices (nominal) rather than real purchasing power; they can distort wages and prices across the economy by altering the value of money. Do not assume a subsidy improves real production or living standards simply because nominal prices or incomes rise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free ports/open trade enrich towns and nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Every town and country, on the contrary, in proportion as they have opened their ports to all nations, instead of being ruined by this free trade...have been enriched by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical/general observation: nations or towns that reduce restrictions and allow broad foreign trade tend to prosper (Holland cited). Policy inclination: prefer openness over protectionism; beware mercantile maxims that aim at impoverishing neighbours.
